It names one premises, an establishment or a site, by its name and at its locality: `place.name` is that name and `place.locality` the town. Or it says plainly, in its title or its summary, that it is a kind of place and names no premises: then `place.name` holds the kind, for example `motel`, and `place.locality` the town. Where you are given places to stay from map data for a town, a premises you name there is one of those, under the name it is given, if any of them fits the party. A kind of place is the fallback, for a town whose list is empty or where nothing in it fits.

Rainfall can raise water levels, and I have not verified crossing depths. Hut fees are an estimate, not a quote.

Access needs: not answered
Budget: shoestring, as a feeling rather than a figure
Appetite for effort: demanding
Roughest night they will accept: rustic
Would rule the trip out: Nothing that requires a river ford above the knee

About this backcountry:

candidatesAccepted.title: Backcountry refuge (hut) in Parc national de la Gaspésie
candidatesAccepted.summary: Rustic Sépaq-run backcountry refuges suit a hut-based, 3-night trip within 16 km days; booked through Sépaq, and late-summer weekends fill early. Access needs were not answered, and I could not check which hut routes avoid fords or exposed, cloud-prone alpine sections; confirm both with the park before choosing.

candidatesAccepted.title: Backcountry campsite as a fallback near huts
candidatesAccepted.summary: If refuges are full, rustic tent sites along the park's trail network keep the trip shoestring-friendly. This needs carrying a tent, which goes beyond the hut-only shelter the party stated. Access needs were not answered.

candidatesAccepted.title: Roadside campground or hostel near the park entrance
candidatesAccepted.summary: A cheap, rustic night by the road before or after the backcountry stretch helps if a long drive from Québec City or poor weather on the ridges changes plans. Access needs were not answered.

candidatesAccepted.title: Mont Jacques-Cartier summit hike
candidatesAccepted.summary: Climb to the highest summit in southern Québec on the alpine tundra, with a chance of seeing the Gaspésie caribou herd; the trail is well marked and staffed. Access to the summit is restricted for caribou protection, with shuttle and timing rules set by Sépaq that vary year to year, so check before you go. Access needs were not answered and are not accounted for.

candidatesAccepted.title: Mont Albert summit and tableland loop
candidatesAccepted.summary: A demanding loop over the serpentine tableland of Mont Albert, with views across the Chic-Chocs. It is very exposed: in cloud, the open tundra is exactly the navigation you said you want to avoid, so treat a clear forecast as a precondition. The loop runs long, and its length against your 480-minute ceiling is not confirmed.

candidatesAccepted.title: Mont Ernest-Laforce wildlife walk
candidatesAccepted.summary: A short, sheltered hike that is often good for moose. It is a low-exposure option for a cloudy day when the high summits are unwise. Access needs were not answered.

candidatesAccepted.title: Lac aux Américains and cirque
candidatesAccepted.summary: A forested trail to a glacial cirque lake below Mont Xalibu. It is mostly below the treeline, so it holds up in poor visibility. Ford depths on park trails were not checked; your knee-depth limit should be confirmed with park staff.

candidatesAccepted.title: Park entry (Sépaq daily access)
candidatesAccepted.summary: Daily access fees apply for each adult. The figures here are approximate and not a quote. Hut nights are booked separately through Sépaq and are not covered here.

candidatesAccepted.title: Mont Jacques-Cartier alpine zone: wind, cloud and closure conditions
candidatesAccepted.summary: The summit plateau above treeline is fully exposed. Fog can drop visibility to a few metres, and late-season wind and cold are real even in August. Access is also restricted around the caribou herd. Because you don't want to navigate in cloud, treat this as a day objective only if the forecast is clear. Check current trail status and caribou-related restrictions with SÉPAQ (Parc national de la Gaspésie) and the forecast with Environment and Climate Change Canada. This is not clearance to go. Access needs were not answered and are not accounted for here.

candidatesAccepted.title: Hut-to-hut stretch below treeline as the bad-weather option
candidatesAccepted.summary: Huts linked by forested trail keep you off exposed ridges if cloud sits on the summits. Daily distances should fit within your 16 km limit. SÉPAQ manages hut reservations and the official stream-crossing information, so confirm with them that no ford above the knee is required in late summer. Rainfall can raise water levels, and I have not verified crossing depths. Hut fees are an estimate, not a quote.

place.name: Parc national de la Gaspésie hut network

candidatesAccepted.title: Kit check for Chic-Choc late-summer weather bands
candidatesAccepted.summary: Expect nights near freezing at altitude by early September, along with wind-driven rain and summit fog. Pack waterproof shells, warm layers and a hat and gloves. Bring a GPS or offline map as a backup, not as a reason to go into cloud. Gaiters help on wet trail, and you should carry hut essentials such as a sleeping bag, stove and water treatment. The Centre de découverte et de services can advise on current trail and weather conditions. This is a gear band only, not a go/no-go.

place.name: Centre de découverte et de services

candidatesAccepted.title: SÉPAQ backcountry hut reservations, Parc national de la Gaspésie
candidatesAccepted.summary: Refuges in the Chic-Chocs must be reserved in advance through SÉPAQ, and late-summer weekends fill early; securing three consecutive hut nights within 16 km legs decides whether the trip happens. The sequence of huts is for the planner to work out, not me. Ford depths on the chosen route were not checked; ask the park whether any crossing could reach above the knee after rain.

place.name: Centre de découverte et de services, Parc national de la Gaspésie

candidatesAccepted.title: Park access fee and backcountry registration
candidatesAccepted.summary: Daily park access fees apply for each person and each day inside the park, and backcountry users register before setting out. Rates for 2027 are not confirmed here.

place.name: Centre de découverte et de services, Parc national de la Gaspésie

candidatesAccepted.title: Offline maps, weather check and satellite messenger rental
candidatesAccepted.summary: There is little or no cell coverage on the high plateaus. Since neither of you wants to navigate in cloud, carry offline maps and a paper map, and check the mountain forecast before leaving. Consider renting a satellite messenger so you can turn back or call for help. I could not confirm local rental availability; Québec City outdoor shops are the likely source.

candidatesAccepted.title: Check that travel/medical insurance covers backcountry rescue
candidatesAccepted.summary: Check that your provincial health plan or other insurance covers evacuation from remote terrain. This is cheap or free to check and matters on a shoestring budget. Access needs were not answered, so I have not accounted for any medical considerations.
